failure_summary.description: The agent misranked claims or rejected an apparently stronger statement without checking whether the hypotheses make it equivalent or directly support its added strength.
The agent guessed an unstated meaning for H(n,m) and selected a congruence condition by plausibility rather than deriving or verifying it.

patch.reasoning: The failures share a need for explicit evidence-based comparison: distinguish abstract properties from constructive claims, avoid promoting aggregate guarantees to componentwise ones, and evaluate equivalence under the full hypotheses rather than relying on generic strength intuition. A separate reminder discourages inventing definitions for unexplained notation.

edits.target: - For an equivalence, check both implications.
edits.content: - In equivalence questions, test both directions under all stated hypotheses; do not reject an apparently stronger asymptotic statement merely because the generic implication is one-way, since the restricted class may force equivalence. Conditions already assumed in the stem are redundant and cannot distinguish the options.

edits.target: - For competing formulas, compare signs, coefficients, factors, index ranges, and wording such as “only one” versus “at most one.” Use definitions to check which terms and indices should appear; when useful, test a low-dimensional case, specialization, or boundary case rather than relying on plausibility.
edits.content: - Do not infer an unfamiliar object's definition from its notation or a guessed application area. Use the definition or presentation supplied, or a reliably identified theorem; never choose a formula merely because it looks more elaborate or plausible. If choices differ by congruences, reduce and compare them exactly.

edits.target: - Separate a claimed conclusion from an offered explanation: a correct conclusion does not by itself establish the proposed mechanism. Once a direct check distinguishes the options, commit rather than adding speculative exceptions.
edits.content: - Compare constructive and abstract claims carefully: an explicitly exhibited compatible metric implies metrizability, but metrizability alone does not supply an explicit construction. Likewise, a bound on total leftover does not imply exact coverage of a named component or a specified location for the leftovers; treat each such add-on as a separate claim requiring direct support.
